Article Title: Present tense, future perfect: Zurich Airport sees 'slower ramp-up' in Noida Airport traffic
Article Text:
Dilli door ast (Photo: Saurabh Sinha)

NEW DELHI: Zurich Airport has prepared itself for a longer takeoff roll at Noida Airport before the traffic here takes off. Multiple factors like the last-minute pullout by on of the three launch airlines; Delhi's IGI Airport operating way below its existing and still expandable capacity and Noida International Airport's (NIA) connectivity woes with Delhi have meant a much lower than originally expected air traffic at the new hub that stated operations on June 15. Zurich Airport International AG is NIA's primary developer and concessionaire.Zurich Airport has said in its outlook for NIA: "Slower ramp up expected due to challenging geo political environment with near time performance remaining subject to elevated uncertainty. Route network will continue to expand with international services expected to follow. Strong confidence in the long term growth potential and attractive fundamentals of the Indian aviation market."It said NIA saw 104 flights and 25,000 passengers in June. This rose to 1,044 flights and 77,000 passengers in July. The airport's HY 16 EBIDTA loss is estimated about $3 million.IndiGo is the biggest operator at NIA, with Akasa having a few flights. Air India Express, which was to be the third launch airlines, had pulled out due to mounting losses of AI group. Setting up a new base means incurring significant expense, something AI wanted to avoid at this time.The going was never going to be easy for NIA, the first second airport to open in an Indian urban conglomerate without either the pre-existing hub operating to capacity (like Mumbai CSMIA); being constrained (like Goa Dabolim) or the older one shutting down (like Bengaluru HAL, Hyderabad Begumpet and Visakhapatnam when Bhogapuram opens in a couple of months). The new airports in Hyderabad and Bengaluru are almost as far as Delhiites find NIA to be but travellers simply didn’t have any option but to trudge the distance. Delhi, Gurgaon, Noida and Ghaziabad, however, have an option that’s closer, better connected and more affordable multi modal transport.When it was coming up amid the boom post Covid boom in air travel, NIA was expected to have a tough time till 2030 when IGIA was to saturate by reaching its peak capacity of about 13-14 crore passengers annually (CPA). IGIA currently has a capacity of 11 CPA and handled less than 8 crore passengers last year.Delhi Airport handles about 1,300 flights daily, way short of the 1,550 seen during the heady days of G20.So NIA would have to compete to get traffic with peak traffic hour slot availability being its USP to attract airlines. But it opened at a time when Indian carriers are reeling under the triple impact of finding lucrative western routes become unviable for them due to closure of Pakistan airspace for them since last April, US-Iran war sending oil prices flaring and the rupee weakening. As a result, they are cutting flights.
Article Summary: Zurich Airport has said in its outlook for NIA: "Slower ramp up expected due to challenging geo political environment" IndiGo is the biggest operator at NIA, with Akasa having a few flights. Delhi Airport handles about 1,300 flights daily, way short of the 1,550 seen during the heady days of G20.

NEW DELHI: A passenger flying from Phuket to Bangalore on Friday allegedly tried to conceal narcotics in the overhead oxygen mask panel of Air India Express flight (IX 903). Sources say he was allegedly carrying 13 packets of contraband substance he had bought in Phuket."He tried to hide them in an overhead panel of the aircraft lav. When he was not able to either do so or conceal the entire stuff with him, he threw some in the lav bin," said sources. We maintain strict protocols and continue to support the authorities in all investigations.”

Article Title: 'Issue of enormous significance': Kharge writes to PM Modi, demands 25-year delimitation freeze
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge on Thursday wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, reiterating the Congress' demand to maintain the existing strength of the Lok Sabha at 543 for another 25 years.Kharge's letter came after Union parliamentary affairs minister hinted at a possible special session of Parliament for the passage of the Delimitation Bill.In his letter, Kharge urged the government to convene an all-party meeting to discuss its proposed delimitation exercise before any such session."I have written to PM Modi on delimitation, the delay in prorogation of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, and the likely special session mentioned by the Union minister of parliamentary affairs in a television interview last evening," Kharge said."I had last written to you on July 16, 2026 requesting you to convene an All-Party meeting for discussing the Government's proposals for delimitation. I had also requested you to give all political parties adequate time to study such proposals in detail before they are introduced in any special session of Parliament that you may be contemplating," he added.Kharge also urged PM Modi to maintain the state-wise strength in Lok Sabha for another 25 years and introduce one-third reservation for women from the 2029 Lok Sabha elections."Maintain the existing strength of the Lok Sabha at 543 for another 25 years; Maintain the existing state-wise strength in the Lok Sabha for another 25 years; "Introduce one-third reservation for women from the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.Kharge reiterated his demand that the government convene an all-party meeting and give political parties and state governments adequate time to examine the proposals."This is an issue that has enormous significance for the country. Please do not again try and bulldoze as you attempted on April 16 and 17, 2026," Kharge said.
Article Summary: Kharge's letter came after Union parliamentary affairs minister hinted at a possible special session of Parliament for the passage of the Delimitation Bill. In his letter, Kharge urged the government to convene an all-party meeting to discuss its proposed delimitation exercise before any such session.

Article Title: Year-wise plan to implement Samudra Manthan in works
Article Text:
Petroleum minister Hardeep Puri reviewed the action taken on decisions from two brainstorming sessions on the rollout of the scheme, which received Cabinet’s approval, said officials. (Photo: IANS)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Government is likely to finalise a year-wise plan soon for drilling, seismic surveys and rig deployment under Samudra Manthan, a Rs 84,084-crore national programme aimed at stepping up oil and gas exploration in India’s offshore basins and reducing dependence on energy imports.Officials said petroleum minister Hardeep Puri recently reviewed the action taken on decisions from two brainstorming sessions held in Gurgaon in Haryana and Duliajan in Assam, on the rollout of the scheme, which received Cabinet’s approval last month.The year-wise roadmap will help government carry out exploration and production activities in a concerted manner across Krishna-Godavari (KG), Mahanadi, Andaman and Cauvery basins and ensure systematic utilisation of funds, an official said.The scheme will fund acquisition, processing and interpretation of seismic data, scientific drilling in frontier basins, accelerated exploration in deepwater and ultra-deepwater blocks, and development of shared offshore production and evacuation infrastructure.While Rs 43,200 crore has been earmarked for drilling 60 exploratory deepwater wells over five years, Rs 28,534 crore has been allocated for acquisition of 2D and 3D seismic data, Rs 10,000 crore for common infrastructure hubs and Rs 2,000 crore for an oil and gas manufacturing and services zone.India’s annual crude oil requirement is around 256 million tonnes (MT), of which nearly 88 per cent is imported. Domestic crude oil production from 26 sedimentary basins is estimated at around 28 MT. With domestic output stagnating even as demand continues to rise, government has been looking to step up exploration to improve energy security and reduce import dependence.Samudra Manthan is expected to add more than 600 million metric tonnes of oil equivalent (MMTOE) to the country’s hydrocarbon reserves and boost domestic production of crude oil and natural gas.Officials said government has implemented a series of upstream sector reforms over the past decade, including opening up almost the entire offshore acreage for exploration, changes to legal and contractual framework, and strengthening National Data Repository. Samudra Manthan would complement these reforms by providing public funding for offshore exploration and facilitating the deployment of advanced technologies, they said.The scheme also includes dedicated provisions for digital programme management, capacity building, technology adoption, stakeholder engagement and international outreach, creating an integrated ecosystem to accelerate offshore exploration and production in the country.
Article Summary: Government is likely to finalise a year-wise plan soon for drilling, seismic surveys and rig deployment under Samudra Manthan. The scheme is aimed at stepping up oil and gas exploration in India’s offshore basins and reducing dependence on energy imports.

Article Title: Caste count method in Census ‘misleading’: Congress letter to PM
Article Text:
The letter from Kharge and Rahul said govt should prepare a fresh questionnaire through consultations with parties.

NEW DELHI: Terming the methodology for caste count adopted in Census 2027 “misleading” as it will not give a headcount of OBCs, leaders of opposition in Parliament, Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi, have written to PM Narendra Modi demanding the Census questionnaire on caste notified recently be abandoned and a new one be drafted. They underlined that the word “OBC” has not even been used in the Census.In the backdrop of the controversy triggered by the questionnaire, Kharge and Rahul told the PM “your govt” has adopted an “open-ended question” to collect information about caste, and enumerators will have to take for an answer whatever a person replies to the caste question. They argued that a caste is known by different names and sub-castes depending on the region, which would result in one caste being recorded by thousands of names. “This would result in lakhs of castes being registered in the country, and the entire data recorded in the caste census would become useless,” the letter said.“We don’t approve of the caste census being done through this methodology. Govt should cancel the present questionnaire and prepare a fresh one through consultations with political parties, experts, and the public so that a correct headcount of every caste and community is collected and the caste census is precise, relevant, and beneficial,” it said.It said a readymade solution to the problem is that a “drop-down menu” comprising a list of castes be added to the questionnaire. “This very methodology is used for counting SCs and STs (in Census)... This methodology was adopted in the surveys of Bihar and Telangana. We are enclosing the caste lists of the two surveys for understanding.” Further, the letter said such a list of castes for Census can easily be compiled on the basis of the existing Socially and Educationally Backward Classes list and data from the Anthropological Survey of India.Releasing the letter, AICC spokesperson Jairam Ramesh and OBC department chairperson Anil Jaihind said govt had, in an affidavit to SC in Sept 2021, submitted that a “drop-down menu” with a list of castes will have to be used if a caste census were to be done. Ramesh said census enumerators can carry the said list of OBCs and record precise answers. He accused govt of “sabotaging” the caste census.
Article Summary: Leaders of opposition in Parliament, Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi, have written to PM Narendra Modi. They underlined that the word "OBC" has not even been used in the Census. They argued that a caste is known by different names and sub-castes depending on the region, which would result in one caste being recorded by thousands of names.

Article Title: Nepal flood: Centre puts Bihar & UP on high alert as NDRF deploys teams
Article Text:
Flash floods in Nepal have triggered alerts in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: In view of the flash flood situation in Nepal, Union home minister Amit Shah Wednesday spoke with CMs of Bihar and UP and assured all help to border districts, including deployment of additional National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams. The administrations of these districts have been put on high alert.“Govt of India stands with Nepal in this hour of crisis. I spoke with CMs of Bihar and UP regarding the disaster in Nepal. In border areas likely to be affected, local administration and rescue teams, along with NDRF, have been placed on high alert,” Shah said on X, expressing condolences to families of those who lost their loved ones in the disaster.Officers of home affairs, external affairs, jal shakti and defence ministries are monitoring the situation.Water level on Nepal-side reservoirs is reducing and the situation is under control. No panic-like situation has arisen, according to Central Water Commission (CWC).NDRF had earlier said the flash floods in the Nepal-China border region has led to a sudden rise in water level in Trishuli river at Furke Khola in Nepal, around 160 km from the Indian border, and the flood wave is likely to travel downstream in Gandak river.“Local authorities in Bihar and UP near the India-Nepal border along Gandak river have been advised to remain alert and maintain close monitoring of the situation,” NDRF said. In close coordination with the states and CWC, NDRF is keeping a close watch on the situation and has kept additional teams on standby for emergent requirements in case of any “unforeseen” situation.Out of nine NDRF teams deployed in Bihar, two have been dispatched for deployment in West Champaran and Muzaffarpur. The state govt is monitoring the situation and, in case of requirement, additional teams will be deployed.
Article Summary: Flash floods in Nepal have triggered alerts in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Water level on Nepal-side reservoirs is reducing and the situation is under control. No panic-like situation has arisen, according to Central Water Commission. NDRF is keeping a close watch on the situation and has kept additional teams on standby for emergent requirements.

Article Title: Nepal floods: Kathmandu agrees to foreign rescue help after pressure; India acts on its 'request'
Article Text:
Rescue teams search for survivors in flood-hit areas of Nepal as authorities seek international assistance

Why Nepal agreed

India dispatches 3rd consignment of aid

Nepal has agreed to accept foreign assistance for rescue operations after initially refusing the same as the scale of devastation from the floods continued to overwhelm relief efforts, The Kathmandu Post reported on Friday.India moved quickly to respond to Kathmandu's request for specialised support. It has sent 11-member team of doctors, paramedics & recce team for tunnel rescue operations.Earlier, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal had said that India had sent the team at Nepal's request. "As requested by Nepal, we are preparing to send a tunnel rescue team, for which a recce team is being flown in first to assess the on-ground situation and what sort of equipment will be required. We are also sending a medical team to Nepal. In addition, we have also offered Bailey bridges along with associated technical teams so that connectivity can be restored quickly in the affected parts of Nepal and we can help in rescue and relief efforts. .. One Bailey bridge is already in Nepal and can be deployed for relief and connectivity efforts,” the MEA spokesperson Jaiswal said.Nepal reversed its earlier decision amid mounting pressure from countries whose nationals remain missing in the flood-hit areas.Several governments had urged Kathmandu to allow their specialist search-and-rescue teams to assist in locating survivors.“We received massive pressure from the international community to allow at least search-and-rescue teams and some experts because their citizens have also gone missing in the floods. We are allowing a limited number of experts in certain areas,” The Kathmandu Post reported quoting a senior government official.The decision also came as rescue operations made limited progress, with dozens of people still unaccounted for inside hydropower tunnels in Rasuwa and Nuwakot. The scale of the disaster has further increased the need for specialised tunnel-rescue expertise.Nepal also has limited capacity for DNA testing and forensic identification of bodies. Foreign experts will therefore assist with identifying the dead and ensuring that remains can be handed over to families as quickly as possible.India also dispatched its third consignment of humanitarian assistance to Nepal. The 10-tonne shipment included portable generators, dignity kits, food packets and water purification tablets, while the 11-member team of doctors, paramedics and tunnel-rescue specialists travelled on the same flight.The latest consignment takes India's total relief assistance to Nepal to 57.5 tonnes since August 26. The earlier shipments included temporary shelters, blankets, hygiene kits, solar lamps, medicines, dewatering pumps, generators, kitchen sets and food supplies.India has also offered Bailey bridges to help restore connectivity, with Jaiswal noting that one such bridge is already in Nepal and can be deployed for relief operations.
Article Summary: India has sent 11-member team of doctors, paramedics & recce team for tunnel rescue operations. India also dispatched its third consignment of humanitarian assistance to Nepal. The 10-tonne shipment included portable generators, dignity kits, food packets and water purification tablets.

Article Title: Government tightens norms for e-cycles, e-bikes
Article Text:
Road transport ministry plans to tighten norms for e-cycles & e-bikes with max speed of 25kmph and motor power below 600 watt.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The road transport ministry has proposed to tighten technical and safety norms for low-speed electric cycles and e-bikes with a maximum speed of 25 kmph and motor power below 600 watts. Manufacturers of these would have to get vehicles certified by authorised testing agencies before they can qualify for exemption from the Motor Vehicles Act to be treated as “motor vehicle”.At present, electric two-wheelers that have motor power below 250 watts are not treated as “motor vehicles” and hence don’t need registration. This definition is now being expanded to vehicles that have motor power up to 600 watts, which officials said is “realistic”.All these vehicles will be required to use only lithium-ion batteries instead of lead-acid batteries.As per draft amendments to Central Motor Vehicles Rules, such vehicles will have to be fitted with “suitable brakes and retro-reflective devices” for visibility. The draft notification said for pedal-assisted electric bicycles, the motor assistance must progressively reduce and cut off once the vehicle reaches 25 kmph or when the rider stops pedalling.The proposal is significant considering that low-speed electric two-wheelers have witnessed rapid growth as affordable urban mobility options, but many models have operated with limited regulatory oversight.
Article Summary: Road transport ministry plans to tighten norms for e-cycles & e-bikes with max speed of 25kmph and motor power below 600 watt. Manufacturers of these would have to get vehicles certified by authorised testing agencies before they can qualify for exemption from the Motor Vehicles Act.

Article Title: The Dalit enigma: Why Mayawati is going solo in Punjab
Article Text:
Mayawati’s solo Punjab gamble tests whether the state’s 32% Dalit population can translate into a consolidated BSP vote.

Punjab's number paradox

In Punjab, Dalits are divided into several sub-castes and religion.

From Kanshi Ram's Punjab to BSP's high-water mark

Mayawati pays tribute on death anniversary of Kanshi Ram.

How 2022 exposed the paradox

SAD and its alliance route

AAP's pitch: Welfare, not identity

Congress has history, but not the Dalit lock

Mayawati's real gamble

Ready to play a spoilsport?

Bahujan Samaj Party ( BSP ) chief Mayawati has decided to go solo in the upcoming 2027 Punjab assembly election. This move has put the spotlight on a striking contradiction in the state's politics: Punjab has India's highest proportion of Scheduled Castes, but no political party has been able to turn that numerical strength into a durable Dalit vote bloc.On August 25, Mayawati announced that the BSP would contest the polls "alone without any alliance or compromise with anyone", arguing that electoral tie-ups risked weakening the party’s vote share and demoralising its cadre.The decision carries particular significance in Punjab, where BSP founder Kanshi Ram began his political journey and where Scheduled Castes account for 31.94% of the population, according to the 2011 Census.Yet nearly one-third of Punjab's population has never translated into nearly one-third of the vote for the BSP - or any other Dalit-centric political formation.Instead, the Dalit electorate has remained divided across caste, religious, regional and economic lines, allowing the Congress, AAP, SAD and BJP to each build pockets of support within it.That makes Mayawati's 2027 gamble less about the size of Punjab's Dalit population and more about a difficult political question: Can she turn the state's 32% Dalit population into a coherent electoral bloc?The numbers explain why every major political party wants a share of the Dalit vote. Punjab had about 88.6 lakh Scheduled Castes in the 2011 Census, accounting for 31.94% of its population - the highest SC proportion among Indian states. The community is particularly concentrated in the Doaba region, which includes Jalandhar, Hoshiarpur and Nawanshahr.Eight of Doaba's 23 assembly constituencies are reserved for SC candidates, while both Lok Sabha constituencies in the region, Jalandhar and Hoshiarpur, are reserved.Across Punjab, 34 of the 117 assembly seats are reserved for Scheduled Caste candidates. But the political influence of Dalit voters extends far beyond these constituencies.A 2021 analysis by Lokniti-CSDS professor Sanjay Kumar found that Dalits accounted for more than 30% of voters in 54 assembly constituencies and between 20% and 30% in another 45.In other words, Dalit voters can influence far more than the 34 seats formally reserved for them.But there is a crucial caveat: 'Dalit' is not a single political identity in Punjab.The community comprises several sub-caste and religious groups, including Ravidassias/Ad-Dharmis, Mazhabi Sikhs, Ramdasias and others. Their geographical distribution, religious affiliations, economic circumstances and political histories differ.That fragmentation has repeatedly prevented the kind of consolidated Dalit politics that emerged around the BSP in Uttar Pradesh.Punjab's agrarian structure adds another layer. Land and economic power remain disproportionately concentrated among dominant agrarian communities, particularly Jat Sikhs. As a result, Dalit politics in the state often revolves around land rights, employment, reservation, social dignity and access to common resources, rather than caste identity alone.The irony is that Punjab was once among the BSP's strongest political laboratories.Kanshi Ram, born in Punjab, built his early political movement around the mobilisation of Scheduled Castes and other marginalised communities before founding the BSP in 1984.The party's breakthrough in Punjab came in the 1992 election. It won nine of the state's 117 seats with 16.32% of the vote, emerging as the principal opposition party in the House. Six of those nine seats came from Doaba, underlining the region’s importance to the party’s political project.But the breakthrough proved difficult to sustain.In 1997, the BSP's tally fell to one seat, although it still secured 7.48% of the vote. Its vote share then declined steadily — to 5.69% in 2002, 4.13% in 2007 and 4.29% in 2012. By 2017, it had fallen to 1.52%.In 2022, the BSP won just one seat with 1.77% of the vote, contesting as part of its alliance with the Shiromani Akali Dal.The steep decline in three decades captures the central problem Mayawati now faces.If the BSP's decline showed the difficulty of sustaining Dalit-centric politics, the 2022 assembly election demonstrated how effectively mainstream parties can cut across caste identities.The AAP won 92 of Punjab's 117 seats with 42.01% of the statewide vote, while Congress was reduced to 18 seats.The AAP’s performance was particularly striking in SC-reserved constituencies. It won 29 of the 34 reserved seats, while Congress won four and the SAD-BSP alliance one.The result also undercut the assumption that Congress's elevation of Charanjit Singh Channi as Punjab's first Dalit CM would automatically consolidate the Dalit vote behind the party. Channi became CM in September 2021, just months before the election. His elevation was widely viewed as an attempt to appeal to the state’s huge Dalit electorate.But in March 2022, Congress suffered a dramatic defeat.The SAD has historically had its own Dalit support base, particularly among Sikh Dalits.Its alliance with Mayawati ahead of the 2022 election was an attempt to combine the Akali network among sections of the Sikh electorate with the BSP's Dalit support base.The combination, however, failed to produce the revival the two parties had hoped for. The alliance won four seats - three for the SAD and one for the BSP - with a combined vote share of around 20%.BJP's gamble: From alliance politics to going soloThe BJP faces perhaps the most difficult social-coalition challenge of all.Its long-standing electoral arrangement with the SAD ended after the Akali Dal walked out of the NDA at the Centre over the farm laws.The BJP is now trying to establish itself as an independent force in a state where it historically relied heavily on the Akali alliance to provide it with a rural and Sikh social base. That means the party needs to build coalitions beyond the constituencies it traditionally relied on, while also trying to repair its relationship with farmers.Dalit voters are an obvious part of that expansion strategy.But Punjab is not Uttar Pradesh or Bihar. There, the BJP has invested heavily in a social coalition involving non-Yadav OBCs and Dalits. A different caste and religious configuration shapes Punjab’s political landscape, while its agrarian structure and Sikh identity make the BJP’s social engineering considerably more complicated.For the BJP, winning Dalit voters is therefore not simply about adding another community to its support base. It is about constructing an entirely new political coalition in a state where its old alliance no longer provides the same electoral cushion.The AAP has already demonstrated why the size of the Dalit population does not automatically translate into BSP votes.In 2022, the party's appeal cut across caste lines, combining welfare, anti-incumbency and the promise of an alternative to the traditional parties. It also had the 'Delhi model' to demonstrate its pitch.AAP sought to build a political vocabulary around BR Ambedkar, combining Ambedkarite symbolism with a broader welfare narrative.Rather than presenting Dalits as a separate electoral constituency, the party has sought to fold their concerns into a larger promise around government schools, healthcare, jobs, welfare delivery and social dignity.However, now the 2027 election will test whether AAP can retain that support after a full term in government.Congress has historically had a strong base among both Hindu and Sikh Dalits in Punjab, but its 2022 performance showed the limits of that advantage. In the 2017 election, the party won 21 of 34 SC-reserved seats; by 2022, after making Charanjit Singh Channi the state’s first Dalit CM and projecting him as its CM face, Congress was reduced to just four reserved seats, while AAP won 29.The setback has not ended Congress's Dalit outreach. In January 2026, Channi himself raised questions within the party over the representation of Dalit leaders, pointing out that several key Punjab Congress positions were held by Jat Sikhs.For Congress, the 2027 challenge is therefore not winning Dalit votes from scratch, but rebuilding a social coalition it once had, without reducing Dalit politics to the Channi factor alone.Mayawati’s decision to contest alone is therefore both ideological and organisational.The BSP has something only a few parties can claim: a political vocabulary explicitly built around Ambedkar, Kanshi Ram and Bahujan mobilisation. Punjab also provides the demographic foundation for such a project.But the party’s electoral history demonstrates the enormous gap between having a potential social constituency and converting it into votes and seats.The challenge is not simply to persuade Dalits to vote for the BSP. It is to persuade different Dalit communities that their interests are sufficiently common to vote for the same party. That is a much harder proposition in Punjab than the 32% figure suggests.There is, however, another reason Mayawati’s decision could matter even if the BSP does not return to anything close to its 1992 performance.Punjab’s 2027 contest is shaping up as a fragmented battle involving AAP, Congress, BJP and SAD, although the possibility of a BJP-SAD reunion remains open.In such a contest, even a relatively small but geographically concentrated BSP vote could become consequential.The party’s past performance offers a warning to the larger parties. In 2024, the BSP was reported to have remained a significant factor in parts of Doaba despite its shrinking statewide base, with observers pointing to its potential to influence contests in seats such as Anandpur Sahib, Jalandhar and Hoshiarpur.That is the paradox of Mayawati's Punjab gamble.The BSP may no longer have the numbers to dominate Punjab’s Dalit politics, but it could still have enough votes to disrupt everyone else’s arithmetic.The 2027 election will therefore test not just whether Mayawati can revive the BSP in Kanshi Ram’s home state, but whether Punjab’s nearly 32% Dalit population can finally translate its demographic weight into political leverage - if not as a single bloc, then as the constituency no major party can afford to ignore.
Article Summary: Bahujan Samaj Party ( BSP ) chief Mayawati has decided to go solo in the upcoming 2027 Punjab assembly election. Punjab has India's highest proportion of Scheduled Castes, but no political party has been able to turn that numerical strength into a durable Dalit vote bloc.

Article Title: Flash floods put focus on India's glacial lakes
Article Text:
An aerial view of damaged structures covered in thick mud and debris following the flash floods at Devighat in Nepal’s Nuwakot

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) disaster in Nepal Wednesday has renewed discussion on India's own strategy and preparedness to mitigate such risk with the presence of approximately 200 high-risk glacial lakes in the Himalayan regions.According to govt's survey of these glacial lakes, Himalayan ranges are host to as many as 7,500 of them - with 10% in Sikkim and of which 25 are considered very high-risk. The study found 4,700 of these glacial lakes situated in Ganga river basin with a catchment area estimated at over 2.5 lakh sqkm, projecting a colossal scale of devastation a single breach could cause.India suffered one of the worst GLOF disasters in recent times when on Oct 3, 2023, glacial rocks of 14.7 cubic meter collapsed in South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, close to midnight, "generating a 20-m high displacement wave", wiping out several hydro power assets and settlements on its way downstream.Krishna Vatsa, member of National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), said the Nepal event illustrates a new dimension of Himalayan disaster risk, though the precise sequence of events is still being scientifically established. "These are cascading hazards: an ice or rock failure can become a debris flow, create a temporary lake and then generate a flash flood. Such events can develop extremely rapidly and may provide very little warning time downstream."India's National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme has marked 195 at-risk glacial lakes and follows five key priorities (assessment, monitoring, early warning, mitigation, community awareness). It needs to be speeded up and scaled up immediately as a priority for national security," said Syed Safi Ahsan Rizvi, an ex-NDMA member.As a response to the Sikkim disaster, Centre had set up a high-level coordination committee on GLOF disaster risk reduction. The initiative, spearheaded by PM's principal secretary PK Mishra, was tasked to host multi-agency deliberations and surveys of such lakes and identify the high-risk ones. Govt also allocated Rs 150 crore for the National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme for four Himalayan states having high-risk glacial lakes.The first meeting of the coordination committee on DRR was held in Nov 2024, when PM's principal secretary expressing his satisfaction on the group's "tri-focal lens: assessment, monitoring, and mitigation". The committee hosted regular meetings and received feedback, which were then formed as part of joint strategy between states and Centre. However, not much is known on follow up actions.Earlier, govt had claimed that multi-agency expeditions were conducted to assess all "A-category" lakes. The teams comprised scientists and officials from NDMA, Central Water Commission, Geological Survey of India, Centre for Development of Advance Computing, ITBP and the Army.

NEW DELHI: Junk foods will soon carry warning labels highlighting high levels of salt, sugar and fat, with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) telling Supreme Court on Friday that it has agreed to red-coloured hexagonal warnings on the front of food packages to help consumers identify products high in specified nutrients of concern.FSSAI conveyed its position through a compliance affidavit filed before Supreme Court in response to the court's Aug 13 order on front-of-pack labelling (FoPL).The move comes after the court pushed Centre to act on the issue, saying, "If the Union does it on its own, well and good, otherwise we shall proceed to pass further directions."Under the framework, products high in specified nutrients would carry prominent red hexagonal warnings reading "HIGH FAT", "HIGH SALT" and/or "HIGH SUGAR", as applicable.FSSAI has agreed to exempt single-ingredient foods such as ghee, edible oil, salt, sugar, jaggery and honey from the proposed warnings, subject to applicable food safety and labelling regulations.The regulator has agreed to implement FoPL in phases, giving the industry time to reformulate products. Article Title: Clean energy push unfair on developing nations: CJI Surya Kant
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: CJI Surya Kant on Friday told Commonwealth Countries that it is unfair that the industrialised countries, who took two centuries to adopt clean energy, are asking the nations in the process of industrialisation to move towards renewable energy within decades.Speaking at the Commonwealth Secretariat in London, CJI Kant said, “Countries that are finally industrialising are being asked to move rapidly towards renewable power, and often made to bear the brunt of criticism when they cannot move fast enough. In comparison, the nations urging that transition spent two centuries building their own strength on coal and oil,” he said.Addressing the common platform for 56 countries on “Policy dialogue on climate justice”, the CJI said the cumulative shift of commonwealth countries to clean energy depends on copper, cobalt and lithium, extraction of which carries environmental and social consequences.Developing countries facing myriad challenges depending on their geographical locations and pushing them towards clean energy at an unrealistic pace could create more challenges than solutions, he warned.Justice Kant said, “The challenge, therefore, is to reconcile the urgency of the clean energy transition with the principles of fairness and shared responsibility that must underpin it.”He said the Supreme Court of India and the HCs have played a significant role in protecting the environment, ecology and its endangered species.He recounted the Zambian HC making a copper mining company liable for polluting water. Commonwealth countries can learn from each other’s experience to bolster efforts towards smoother transition towards clean energy without making their populations pay a heavy price, he said.“We need not develop a separate jurisprudential vocabulary in every country where a climate question reaches the Courts. Rather, the Courts should be open to borrowing ideas, approaches, and solutions that have proved useful elsewhere in the Commonwealth, while adapting them carefully to their own constitutional, social, and environmental circumstances,” he said.“Courts must be willing to search for solutions that protect the environment without losing sight of the legitimate needs of development, and to recognise that the two need not always be cast as choices in which one must defeat the other,” CJI Kant said.He cited the case before SC where the officials were accused of felling many trees to widen a road for access to a super specialty hospital for wounded para-military forces. “We had no wish to reward officials who had cut trees; equally, we had no wish to deny wounded soldiers an ambulance route,” he said.Instead of halting the widening of roads, the SC had ordered extensive compensatory afforestation. “We still monitoring that afforestation today… development and preservation do not always have to stand on opposite sides of the scales. Sometimes, the task of a Court is to find the third way to promote both routes through judicial creativity,” he said.
Article Summary: CJI Surya Kant said it is unfair that the industrialised countries, who took two centuries to adopt clean energy, are asking the nations in the process of industrialisation to move towards renewable energy within decades. He said the Commonwealth countries can learn from each other’s experience to bolster efforts towards smoother transition.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court is scheduled to hear a petition on August 31 seeking a directive to the Centre and others to ensure mandatory and uniform labelling on every dispensing nozzle at petrol pumps, disclosing the exact percentage of ethanol in petrol.According to the apex court's causelist of August 31, the plea would come up for hearing before a bench comprising Justices M M Sundresh and authorities to formulate and publish within a time-bound period a transparent transition framework for legacy and non-compatible vehicles, including consideration of designated availability of lower Article Title: UNCCD concludes COP17 with new drought resilience and land restoration initiatives

NEW DELHI: The seventeenth session of the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) conference concluded in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, on Friday by presenting a new global architecture for drought resilience that will help countries bridge the gap between plans and implementation.Multiple new initiatives were announced during the 12-day conference (COP17). They include $1.3 billion in new and pipeline finance for land restoration and strengthening drought resilience in vulnerable countries.These initiatives — the world’s first Drought Resilience Index (DRI) and the Drought Resilience Investment Facility (DRIF) — will help countries in assessing their capacity to anticipate, prepare for and adapt to drought, and unlock much larger flows of institutional and private finance for projects that strengthen water security, sustainable agriculture, nature-based solutions and land restoration.DRI’s technical monitoring metrics will enable countries to identify vulnerabilities and inform more effective policies and investments. Its new AI-powered features can help policymakers, technical experts and the public interpret complex data and turn it into practical insights.DRIF, on the other hand, aims to mobilise up to $400 million in public and private capital for drought resilience. The facility, launched by UNCCD and Luxembourg, will use public capital to reduce investment risks.“We came to Ulaanbaatar saying that COP17 must be a COP of implementation. We leave with more of the architecture needed to make that possible: political decisions, stronger science, innovative financing mechanisms, investment pipelines and partnerships that can move solutions to scale,” said UNCCD executive secretary Yasmine Fouad.The conference took place against a stark global backdrop as up to 40 percent of the world’s land is degraded, while countries have committed to restoring more than one billion hectares, including 26 million hectares by India, by 2030. India was represented by a team led by Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav at COP17.

These are people of Indian origin who may have gone for Kailash Mansarovar Yatra , but they hold other nationalities," Jaiswal said.Jaiswal said around 400 Indian nationals stranded on the Chinese side of the Nepal-China border are safe, with the Indian Embassy in Beijing and local authorities working to facilitate their evacuation.“On the Chinese side, we have 400 Indian nationals. He added that the embassy had been in contact with several of them, while their relatives had also reached out through helpline numbers operated by the mission in Beijing.“Our embassy is in touch with local authorities in China, and they are working out as to how these people who are there can be evacuated,” he said.Jaiswal also said India began sending humanitarian assistance to Nepal on August 26, with the first aircraft carrying 10 tonnes of relief material, including temporary shelters, blankets, hygiene kits, solar lamps and medicines.A second aircraft departed on August 27 carrying 37.5 tonnes of relief supplies, including tents, blankets, hygiene kits, solar lamps, dewatering pumps, kitchen sets, generators, medicines and food items.“We are considering the third flight, expected to leave this evening,” Jaiswal said. The aircraft is expected to carry around 12-13 tonnes of supplies, including portable generators, dignity kits, food, water-purification tablets and medicines requested by the Nepali authorities.A glacier collapse in Tibet triggered severe flash floods and mudslides along the China-Nepal border, killing at least 475 people and leaving several others missing, according to authorities in the two countries. The casualty figures differ between agencies due to variations in data collection, verification and coordination.
Article Summary: 21 Indian nationals from Tamil Nadu who had arrived in Kathmandu from the flood- affected area on Thursday were brought back to Delhi on Friday. 63 Indian nationals working at the Trishuli One hydropower project were also rescued on Thursday. 320 Indian nationals are being treated as missing or uncontactable.

Article Title: 61% of children in India exposed to one more month of heat stress due to climate change: Study
Article Text:
File photo: Heatwave in India

NEW DELHI: In India, 61 per cent of children, or 145 million, are exposed to at least one additional month of heat stress due to climate change every year, new global research has estimated.Findings published in the journal Science Advances show that climate change has doubled the number of children aged up to nine exposed to at least five total months of dangerous heat stress per year -- from 59 million to 118 million (50 per cent of children).An international team of researchers, led by those at Vrije Universiteit Brussel in Belgium, said the study is the first-ever analysis quantifying how heat exposure directly linked to climate change affects different age groups globally, both now and in the near future.Excess heat disrupts the human body's normal functioning, aggravates underlying diseases, and can lead to serious complications such as heatstroke, dehydration, and organ failure.The study focuses on humid heat, which is more dangerous than dry heat because it impedes the body's ability to sweat to cool back down, leading to dangerous levels of heat stress.Globally, up to 560 million children aged 0-9 -- 43 per cent of all children in this age group -- are living through at least one additional month of heat stress per year due to human-induced climate change, the analysis found.The exposure outpaces that for any other age group and is nearly triple the 190 million people (30 per cent) aged 60-69 experiencing the additional health threat, the researchers said.They added climate change is increasing humid heat the most in tropical regions and poorer countries, where populations are younger, and more children are therefore affected.South Asia, Southeast Asia, and West Africa are the regions with the highest number of children exposed to dangerous heat stress today, the team said."Climate change is already causing hundreds of millions of children to suffer from dangerous heat worldwide, posing severe risks to their health. Children in developing countries face (a) disproportionate exposure to climate extremes now and into the future, despite contributing the least to historical greenhouse gas emissions," lead author Rosa Pietroiusti, a PhD researcher at Vrije Universiteit Brussel, said."At the same time, poverty, inadequate housing, limited access to cooling, and overstretched health care systems leave many children with few ways to protect themselves from the heat," Pietroiusti said.The number of children affected by an additional month of dangerous heat is expected to increase to 620 million (49 per cent of all children) and 650 million (59 per cent) children under projected climate change scenarios of 1.5 degrees Celsius and 2 degrees Celsius of global warming, respectively.In India, 166 million children (74 per cent) are projected to experience at least one additional month of heat stress per year under a global warming of 1.5 degrees Celsius.The figure could be 169 million children (96 per cent) under a global warming of 2 degrees Celsius.
Article Summary: In India, 61 per cent of children, or 145 million, are exposed to at least one additional month of heat stress due to climate change every year. South Asia, Southeast Asia, and West Africa are the regions with the highest number of children exposed to dangerous heat stress.

Article Title: From Tagore's thread of unity to booming trade opportunity - how Raksha Bandhan became Rs 25k-crore business
Article Text:
From Tagore's streets to 10-minute delivery: The business of Rakhi

When Tagore turned a ritual into protest

A festival with a turnover

Threads with a message, threads with a name

A thread for every trend

Minutes, not days

The vendors left behind

Opportunity online, obstacles offline

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A hundred and twenty years of the same thread

In August 1905, as Bengal braced for a partition designed by the British to split its Hindu and Muslim population along communal lines, Rabindranath Tagore walked through the streets of Kolkata asking strangers to tie threads on each other's wrists. It was Raksha Bandhan, and Tagore had repurposed a domestic ritual, sisters protecting brothers, into a public act of protest. Hindus tied rakhis on Muslims, Muslims tied them on Hindus, and for one day at least, the colonial administration's attempt to engineer division through the Bengal Partition met a street-level answer in silk thread. The gesture was Tagore's response to a strategy of divide and rule that he saw threatening the nationalist movement at its foundations; the rakhi, in his hands, stopped being only a family custom and became a symbol of a shared, non-negotiable bond between communities.More than a century later, the thread has kept its symbolism but acquired a balance sheet. Raksha Bandhan is now one of the biggest festival-linked retail events in the Indian calendar, and the story of how it got there says as much about India's e-commerce boom, its gig economy and its small-manufacturing base as it does about siblings and sentiment.The Confederation of All India Traders (CAIT) estimates that India’s rakhi trade could reach nearly Rs 25,000 crore this year.The broader Raksha Bandhan-related trade, including sweets, dry fruits, gifts, apparel, electronics, decorative items, puja articles and other festive products, is expected to cross Rs 30,000 crore nationally. Delhi alone is estimated to account for around Rs 4,000 crore, with major markets such as Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazaar, Karol Bagh, Lajpat Nagar, Kamla Nagar, Rajouri Garden, Gandhi Nagar, Khari Baoli and Laxmi Nagar seeing increased shopping activity ahead of Raksha Bandhan. These figures are CAIT estimates based on inputs from traders and trade associations, rather than audited market data.Much of the physical production still runs through India's traditional craft clusters. Kolkata remains a major wholesale and manufacturing hub, supplying rakhi traders across the country. Khadi rakhis from Nagpur, Sanganeri prints from Jaipur, seed rakhis from Pune, tea-leaf rakhis from Assam, jute rakhis from Kolkata, and bamboo and Madhubani-art rakhis from Bihar now sit alongside mass-produced options, driven in part by women's self-help groups and artisan collectives for whom the rakhi season is a source of supplementary household income.What has changed most visibly is the design vocabulary. This year's rakhi shelves carry threads built around Viksit Bharat, BrahMos and women's-empowerment themes alongside the more familiar Rudraksha, Swastik and Bhaiya-Bhabhi pairs, a sign of how quickly manufacturers now respond to the news cycle and government messaging, treating the rakhi as a wearable billboard as much as a ritual object. Superhero and cartoon-branded rakhis for children, evil-eye designs marketed as fashion accessories that can be worn past the festival, and premium metal or stone-studded pieces round out a market that has moved well beyond plain thread.Personalisation has become the dominant pitch, and not just at the top end.Sellers now routinely offer rakhis with a brother's name sublimated onto acrylic or wood, or a sibling photograph printed directly onto the pendant, products that would have required a jeweller or an artist a decade ago and are now templated, priced from under Rs 50 apiece, and turned around in bulk by small manufacturing units in cities such as Ahmedabad, Delhi and Jaipur. The wider gifting trend has moved the same way: industry trackers this year note a decline in generic mass-market combo set, the standard thread-plus-sweets hamper, in favour of curated boxes that buyers can customise by age, taste or budget, from wellness kits to eco-friendly packaging.The most disruptive change, though, has been in delivery. Quick-commerce platforms have turned the rakhi thali, once assembled by a sister at home or bought over a shop counter, into a same-day, sometimes same-hour order: thread, roli-chawal, sweets and a small gift bundled and dispatched from a neighbourhood dark store. For siblings living in different cities, or those who simply left the shopping too late, this has effectively replaced the courier parcels and last-minute market runs of previous years.That speed now comes with an asterisk. Since January this year, the quick-commerce platforms have all dropped explicit "10-minute" delivery claims from their branding, after the Union Labour Ministry pushed quick-commerce companies to stop advertising rigid delivery windows, citing rider safety concerns following gig-worker protests. Blinkit's tagline shifted from promising goods "in 10 minutes" to simply listing what it delivers; some of them now advertise "groceries in minutes" rather than a fixed number. The underlying model, dark stores, real-time inventory, delivery fleets built for speed, is unchanged, and rakhi orders still move fast during the festival rush; platforms have simply stopped putting a number on it.For the street sellers who used to own this season, the shift has been harder to absorb than a change in app copy. Rakesh, who sells rakhi threads and thalis from a stall in one of Delhi's older markets, has watched the balance of the trade move online over the past few years."The availability of Rakhi threads and thalis online have changed things a lot for us," he said. "People get things delivered in minutes, there is also the aspect of personalisation. Customers can get their money back if they do not like a design but that is not the case for us. The demand has not dropped dramatically but we can definitely sense a shift now."His account captures something the trade-body turnover figures don't: this isn't a market in collapse so much as one being quietly redistributed. Total demand for rakhis hasn't fallen, traders' projections for this year are, if anything, higher than last year's, but a growing share of it is being captured by platforms that can offer instant refunds, endless design catalogues and delivery to a doorstep hundreds of kilometres away, none of which a pavement stall can match. A street vendor operates on thin, fixed margins and cannot offer the kind of no-questions-asked returns that have become standard on e-commerce and quick-commerce apps; a design that doesn't suit a customer is a sunk cost for him in a way it isn't for a platform with centralised inventory. What he is describing is less a festival in decline than a festival whose profits are migrating toward whoever controls speed, choice and convenience, the same forces reshaping most other categories of Indian retail.The same platforms squeezing street vendors have opened a door for a different kind of small operator: the home-run, social-media-first rakhi business. Instagram and WhatsApp catalogues have made it possible for someone with no shop and little capital to sell personalised or handcrafted rakhis directly to customers, without a physical stall or a wholesaler in between.But reach isn't the same as revenue, says says a woman running an online rakhi business. "The biggest opportunity is using social media to reach more customers and promote products," she said. "But the biggest challenges for a new small business are building a customer base, increasing sales, competing with larger companies and recovering costs. When sales are low in the initial stages, profits can be very small, or there may be no profit at all.It's a reminder that the barriers for small players haven't disappeared with the shift online — they've simply moved. A social media page can put a home business in front of thousands of potential buyers, but it competes in the same feed as established D2C brands and marketplace sellers with bigger budgets, faster fulfilment and the cushion to absorb a slow first season. For someone starting out, the gap between visibility and an actual, sustainable customer base can take more than one festival cycle to close.The distance between Tagore's Kolkata processions and this year's app-driven rush is, on the surface, total: one was a deliberate refusal of commerce, staged to make a political point about unity in the face of engineered division; the other is commerce itself, organised around choice, speed and margin. But the thread running between them, literally, is the same one: an ordinary domestic ritual, elastic enough to be pressed into whatever a moment demands, whether that moment calls for resistance or for a same-day delivery slot. What has changed is not the rakhi but who gets to decide what it means, and increasingly, that decision is being made by whoever can get it to your wrist the fastest.
Article Summary: Raksha Bandhan is one of the biggest festival-linked retail events in the Indian calendar. The Confederation of All India Traders estimates that India’s rakhi trade could reach nearly Rs 25,000 crore this year. The broader Raksha Bandham- related trade, including sweets, dry fruits, gifts, apparel, electronics, decorative items, puja articles and other festive products, is expected to cross Rs 30,000. crore nationally.

Ramesh targets Centre over free online coaching plan

Existing free coaching scheme misses target

Rahul Gandhi's student campaign

NEW DELHI: Congress MP Jairam Ramesh on Friday slammed the Centre over its recent digital education initiatives, alleging that the government was pushed into announcing free online coaching after Rahul Gandhi highlighted the rising burden of private coaching on Indian families.Ramesh questioned the Centre's ability to implement such schemes, citing a parliamentary panel report that found the existing free coaching programme had achieved only 26 per cent of its enrolment target.In a post on X, Ramesh accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government of attempting to deflect attention from deeper problems in India's education system by turning to online coaching instead of strengthening public education."Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi at the Chhatron ki Goonj event in Kota on June 17th 2026, raised one of the most important issues in education today: that an extractive coaching industry has supplanted the public education system and that Indian families are now spending 2.5 times more on coaching centres than the Govt of India invests in education."Ramesh claimed that Rahul Gandhi's disclosure was followed by the Prime Minister's announcement of free online coaching for students on August 15."It was this disclosure that forced the Prime Minister, in a desperate attempt to escape growing public pressure, to announce free online coaching for students on 15th August. But his Government's track record hardly inspires any confidence. Its existing Free Coaching scheme has been missing its target for 3 years," he said.Ramesh cited the latest report of the parliamentary standing committee of the ministry of social justice and empowerment, tabled on August 10, to question the government's record on its existing free coaching scheme."The Ministry of Social Justice was to enrol 10,500 candidates for free coaching over 3 years, but it has only enrolled 2,790 students - just 26% of the target. The budget for this scheme has reduced every year, and last year's spending was less than half the budget. These startling facts have been revealed in the latest report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, tabled on Aug 10, 2026," he wrote.The Congress leader argued that the government's focus should be on fixing structural weaknesses in the education system rather than expanding digital coaching initiatives."Rather than fundamentally fix India's broken education system or re-invest in public education, the Prime Minister has decided to instead invest public resources in online coaching. It is an accountability-evading gimmick, and this Government has already shown little capacity to implement this scheme successfully," Jairam Ramesh wrote.Ramesh's criticism follows Rahul Gandhi's wider campaign highlighting concerns faced by students, including rising education costs, examination irregularities, paper leaks, recruitment issues and unemployment.The Congress leader launched the 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' campaign in 2026 to bring student concerns into the national political discourse. The campaign has been held in Kota, Dehradun and Prayagraj, among other places.At a recent 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' programme in Maharashtra, Rahul also spoke about the role of women in India, describing them as the country's biggest strength."Women are the strength of India - its foundation, its present, and its future.""You belong to no one but yourself. Be loud. Be proud. Fight for your space. Smash the patriarchy!" he said in a post on X.Addressing the programme, Rahul Gandhi said India's greatest strength lay in the aspirations and potential of its women."Many times, people ask me, 'What is India's biggest strength?' You get many answers when you ask this question. Somebody will say our economy. Somebody will say our military. Somebody will say our medical system. Somebody might even say our people, but I am very clear on what is India's biggest strength, our biggest asset, and that strength is 70 crore unique journeys, unique imaginations, unique dreams that the women of India are living," he said.

Article Title: Expert’s opinion to HC contradicts govt stand on patented cancer drug
Article Text:
Palbociclib is a generic breast cancer drug

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Contradicting the government claim that generic breast cancer drug palbociclib can be used as an alternative to patented drugs in the same group, noted oncologist and Magsaysay award winner Dr R Ravi Kannan has opined that these drugs are not interchangeable. He explained that ribociclib benefits early-stage breast cancer and can reduce recurrence and improve overall survival, while palbociclib trials have shown that it has no role in early breast cancer treatment.Dr Kannan, the director of Cachar Cancer Hospital and Research Centre, Silchar, a nonprofit hospital that provides free cancer treatment, gave his opinion in a case before the Kerala High Court filed by a patient seeking access to expensive patented breast cancer drugs. After the patient’s death, the court took it up suo moto in public interest. It concerned the most common breast cancer subtype, hormone receptor positive and HER2-negative tumors.The petition sought a government use licence under section 100 of the Patent Act, to enable access to ribociclib, a patented drug, at affordable prices. However, government refused to issue a government use licence stating that breast cancer did not constitute a matter of national emergency and that the National Cancer Institute in Jhajjar, and Chittaranjan National Cancer Institute in Kolkata had said that generic palbociclib could be used as an alternative to ribociclib.Dr Kannan’s letter stated that despite palbociclib, abemaciclib and ribociclib being CDK4/6 inhibitors, they “cannot be interchanged in the early breast cancer (adjuvant) setting”. He cited the trial which showed that adding abemaciclib to endocrine therapy significantly reduced recurrence, and extended follow up of seven years showed significant invasive disease-free survival and improved overall survival. He also cited trials that found that giving ribociclib for three years along with non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor, a type of hormone therapy drug used to treat hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, significantly improved the outcomes. The trial showed significant improvement in invasive disease-free survival and reduction in recurrence of the cancer in parts of the body far from the original breast tumor. He added that two large trials had shown that palbociclib in early breast cancer did not show similar advantages.Citing the trial results, Dr Kannan stated that the approval of generic palbociclib in India should not be seen as providing an equivalent adjuvant option. “Clinicians must use the evidence-based drugs--abemaciclib or ribociclib--when indicated for high risk early-stage patients, since palbociclib’s adjuvant trials showed no benefit,” stated the letter.He pointed out that the high cost of abemaciclib and ribociclib meant that vast numbers of high-risk patients who could benefit from these drugs simply could not obtain them. Ribociclib is over Rs 78,400 per month and Abemaciclib Rs 47,700 to 95,500 per month.“Generic entry has historically been the single most reliable lever for expanding access to targeted cancer therapies in resource-limited settings, and there is no clinical reason to expect abemaciclib and ribociclib to be an exception,” stated Dr Kannan adding that only by substantially lowering prices can the lifesaving benefits of these drugs reach the broad population of high-risk patients in India.The latest affidavit submitted on August 14 by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), the apex regulator for pharmaceuticals in India, includes tables that show that both palbociclib and ribociclib are approved for HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer. But the affidavit also records a separate January 2026 approval for ribociclib for early-stage breast cancer in patients at high risk of recurrence. “CDSCO’s own data shows an additional early-stage breast cancer indication for ribociclib that is not shown for palbociclib. Yet the affidavit then says the two medicines have been approved for the same indications. This is a serious contradiction. A drug regulator has a responsibility to place clear and accurate information before the court, particularly when women’s access to life-saving treatment is at stake,” said Gargeya Telakapalli, co-ordinator, Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments.“Nearly one lakh women are dying of breast cancer every year. If that is not a public health emergency, what is? This case has been going on since 2022. The woman who first approached the Court died before she could get the medicine she needed. Many more women have died while this case has continued. The government cannot keep treating access to breast cancer medicines as an ordinary pricing dispute. Women need the best available treatment when it can still save their lives,” said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group.
Article Summary: Dr R Ravi Kannan has opined that these drugs are not interchangeable. He explained that ribociclib benefits early-stage breast cancer and can reduce recurrence and improve overall survival. Palbocic lib trials have shown that it has no role in early breast cancer treatment.

Article Title: India’s GLOF panel working on disaster mitigation at 200 high-risk glacial lakes
Article Text:
India has already suffered one of the worst GLOF disasters in recent times when, on Oct 3, 2023, glacial rocks of 14.7 cubic meters collapsed in South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) disaster in Nepal on Wednesday has renewed discussion on India’s own strategy and preparedness to mitigate such risk, with the presence of approximately 200 high-risk glacial lakes in the Himalayan regions.According to the government’s survey of these glacial lakes, the Himalayan ranges are host to as many as 7,500 glacial lakes, of which 10% are in Sikkim alone. While their mapping revealed that the Ganga River basin has more than 4,700 glacial lakes, from its origin to the foothills of the Himalayas, covering a catchment area of nearly 2.5 lakh sq km, the 25 most at risk are in Sikkim.India has already suffered one of the worst GLOF disasters in recent times when, on Oct 3, 2023, glacial rocks of 14.7 million cubic meters collapsed in South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, close to midnight, generating a “20m high displacement wave”, wiping out several hydropower assets and settlements on its way downstream.In response, the Centre had set up a high-level coordination committee on GLOF disaster risk reduction. The initiative, spearheaded by PM’s principal secretary PK Mishra, was tasked with hosting multi-agency deliberations and surveys of such lakes and identifying the high-risk ones. The Centre also allocated Rs 150 crore for the National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme for four Himalayan states having high-risk glacial lakes.The first meeting of the coordination committee on DRR was held in November 2024, when the PM’s principal secretary expressed his satisfaction with the group’s “tri-focal lens — assessment, monitoring, and mitigation”. The committee hosted regular meetings and received feedback, which then formed part of a joint strategy between states and the Centre. Not much is known on follow up developments.Earlier, the government had claimed that multi-agency expeditions were conducted to assess all A-category lakes, comprising scientists and officials from NDMA, Central Water Commission, Geological Survey of India, Centre for Development of Advanced Computing, Indo-Tibetan Border Police and the Army. The Centre’s Rs 150 crore allocations were used for mitigation measures at five lakes in Sikkim and others.Previous efforts of GLOF risk reduction by setting up two solar-powered twin-camera Automated Weather Stations (AWS) at South Lhonak and Shako Cho in Sikkim had not been very effective. This was supposed to feed vital data to authorities and work as an early warning system. The Centre is currently preparing a “Risk Mitigation Programme which incorporates setting up solar-powered AWS and early warning systems (EWS) at all high-risk glacial lakes.
Article Summary: Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) disaster in Nepal has renewed discussion on India’s own strategy and preparedness to mitigate such risk. India has already suffered one of the worst GLOF disasters in recent times when, on Oct 3, 2023, glacial rocks of 14.7 million cubic meters collapsed in South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim.

Article Title: India & China announce 8-point boundary consensus before Xi's visit, target early & substantial harvest in border delimitation
Article Text:
According to the joint statement, both sides agreed that any situation on the ground would be addressed promptly.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India and China jointly announced Wednesday that the Special Representatives (SR) dialogue on the boundary question - co-chaired by Ajit Doval and Wang Yi this week - had led to an 8-point consensus, signalling some positive progress in boundary talks ahead of President Xi Jinping's visit to India next month.These included advancing consultations for an "early and substantial harvest" of boundary delimitation, setting up more meeting points and hotlines to improve border management, improving understanding of LAC and addressing ground situation through diplomatic and military engagements, expanding trans-border trade and rivers cooperation. The consensus was announced in a rare joint statement after the SR talks.Building upon the outcomes from the last round of talks in 2024, the 2 sides agreed that the Expert Group on Boundary Delimitation and Working Group on Border Management would advance discussions on an “Early and Substantial Harvest” of boundary delimitation and Border Management. The first task for both these groups would be to agree on their respective Terms of Reference, said the joint statement.India and China had agreed last year to set up an expert group under the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs (WMCC), to explore early harvest in boundary delimitation in the India-China border areas.The formulation was changed to early and substantial on this occasion.Two additional meeting points for military talks and 2 more channels of border military hotlines in the Eastern and Middle Sectors were agreed upon to reinforce border management measures, according to both sides.“The two sides underlined their commitment to advancing negotiations on a framework for the settlement of the boundary question in accordance with the Agreement on Political Parameters and Guiding Principles for Settlement of the India-China Boundary Question signed in 2005 and the consensus reached in subsequent SR Talks in pursuit of a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable solution,” said the MEA in a statement. Unlike the Chinese readout of the talks on Tuesday, the joint statement did not mention package settlement or solution, although the 2005 agreement talks about making adjustments to reach a package settlement.The two sides also reaffirmed their commitment to upholding the guidance received from Modi and Xi, maintaining peace and tranquility in the border areas and creating an atmosphere for healthy and steady development of bilateral relations.According to the joint statement, both sides agreed that any situation on the ground would be addressed promptly through existing diplomatic and military channels, including the WMCC, local commander‑level meetings and other agreed mechanisms, to resolve outstanding issues and avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation along the LAC. “The two sides discussed ways to improve understanding of LAC in appropriate areas, for better border management,” said the joint statement.Both sides also noted the progress on trans-border cooperation, with the Indian side appreciating the efforts made by the Chinese side to increase the number of batches of Indian official pilgrimage Kailash-Manasarovar Yatra (KMY) in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China.“Both sides appreciated the reopening of the three designated border trading points. The two sides agreed to strengthen exchanges and cooperation in border trade, pilgrimage and other areas, with the view to work together to create an atmosphere featuring dialogue, peace, consultation and cooperation in the border areas,” said the joint statement.India and China also agreed to hold the next meeting of the India-China Expert-Level Mechanism on Trans-border Rivers in September and maintain communication on issues including hydrological data sharing, and renewal of the relevant MoUs. It’s important for India that China shares hydrological information during emergency situations based on humanitarian considerations. The two sides agreed to hold the 26th round of SR Talks in India in 2027.
Article Summary: India and China jointly announced Wednesday that the Special Representatives (SR) dialogue on the boundary question had led to an 8-point consensus. The consensus signalling some positive progress in boundary talks ahead of President Xi Jinping's visit to India next month. The two sides agreed to hold the 26th round of SR Talks in India in 2027.

Article Title: 3 lakh tonnes of refined sugar to enter market
Article Text:
An official said ex-mill prices increasing from Rs 48 per kg to Rs 58-60 per kg in just a few days showed that speculation and stocking were the main reasons behind the price spike.

NEW DELHI: In what could improve availability of sugar in the market immediately and bring down prices, around 3-3.5 lakh tonnes available with Indian sugar refiners, who import raw sugar duty-free and export it after processing, is likely to come into the domestic market following a recent govt decision.Last week, govt had allowed duty-free import of 10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar and also allowed the processors to sell some refined sugar, which was meant for export only, in the domestic market. Officials and industry insiders said at least 3 lakh tonnes of processed sugar could come into the market quickly. The subsequent import of 10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar will help tide over any supply issue.Meanwhile, the ex-mill price of sugar has gone down by 20% in the past 10 days. Industry sources and officials said the ex-mill price in Kolhapur fell to Rs 48 per kg Wednesday and was around Rs 53 a kg in Uttar Pradesh.An official said ex-mill prices increasing from Rs 48 per kg to Rs 58-60 per kg in just a few days showed that speculation and stocking were the main reasons behind the price spike, and there had been no shortage.Deepak Ballani, director general of Indian Sugar Mills Association, the country’s top sugar industry body, said that govt measures to rationalise sugar prices had started showing results. “Over the last few days, ex-mill sugar prices have declined by nearly 20%, and we expect this reduction to be reflected in retail prices very soon. There is adequate availability of sugar in the country, and consumers will get the commodity at reasonable prices during the forthcoming festive season,” he added.On Wednesday, the average retail price of sugar was Rs 65 per kg.
Article Summary: Around 3-3.5 lakh tonnes available with Indian sugar refiners, who import raw sugar duty-free and export it after processing, is likely to come into the domestic market. Last week, govt had allowed duty- free import of 10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar and also allowed the processors to sell some refined sugar.

Article Title: As obesity rises, Supreme Court puts govt on notice over junk food labels
Article Text:
Number of overweight school-going kids and adolescents increased from 2% to 10% between 2000 and 2022.
